title: The history of the microwave oven
tagline: 160 years from a physicist's equations and wartime radar to the humming box that reheats dinner in two minutes.
intro: In the 1860s a Scottish physicist predicted invisible waves of electricity and magnetism, and soon scientists in Germany and India were making them. Engineers in the US, Europe and Japan then built tubes called magnetrons that could pump out short waves, and in 1940 two scientists in Birmingham made one powerful enough for radar. After the war, a radar engineer noticed that the same waves could cook food. It took Japanese factories, cheap magnetrons and new safety rules to shrink a fridge-sized machine into a box on almost every kitchen counter.

eras.name: Invisible waves
eras.summary: Scientists predict and then make electromagnetic waves. Inventors in the US, Europe and Japan build the first magnetrons, tubes that turn electricity into radio waves.

eras.name: Radar and war
eras.summary: A powerful new magnetron from Birmingham makes short-wave radar possible. It crosses the Atlantic in secret, and American factories make it by the thousand.

eras.name: From radar to restaurant
eras.summary: A radar engineer finds that microwaves cook food. The first ovens are as big as fridges and cost as much as a car, so they go to restaurants, ships and trains.

eras.name: A box on every counter
eras.summary: Ovens shrink onto the countertop, Japanese factories make cheap magnetrons, safety rules calm people's fears, and microwave food fills the shops.

eras.name: A world of microwaves
eras.summary: Smarter electronics give ovens gentler power, China becomes the world's microwave factory, and the appliance spreads to new kitchens in Asia and beyond.

events.title: Light is a wave of electricity and magnetism
events.text: Maxwell, a Scottish physicist, wrote down a set of equations that tie electricity and magnetism together. They showed that the two could travel through space as a wave, and that light itself is one of these waves. His equations also said there should be waves much longer than light, which no one had seen yet.
events.why: Microwaves are one of the invisible waves Maxwell's equations predicted.

events.title: Making invisible waves on purpose
events.text: Hertz made sparks jump across a gap and found that a small loop of wire across the room sparked too. Invisible waves were crossing the room. He showed they bounce and bend like light, just as Maxwell had predicted.
events.why: It proved electromagnetic waves were real, and the unit of frequency, the hertz, is named after him.

events.title: Very short waves through two walls
events.text: Bose built his own transmitter, horn antennas and detectors for waves only millimetres long, at about 60 GHz. In a public demonstration he sent them 23 m, through two walls, to ring a bell and set off a little gunpowder. An IEEE Milestone plaque now honours the work.
events.why: He showed that very short radio waves could be made, aimed and detected, decades before radar.

events.title: A magnet bends the electrons
events.where: General Electric, Schenectady, New York, USA
events.text: Hull studied a vacuum tube with a wire in the middle, a metal cylinder around it and a magnet outside. The magnet bends the electrons flying from the wire so they curl round instead of reaching the cylinder. He published papers and patents on this tube, now called a magnetron.
events.why: Electrons spinning in a magnetic field are still the heart of every microwave oven's magnetron.

events.title: The magnetron starts to sing
events.text: Working separately, the Czech physicist Žáček and the German physicist Habann found that a magnetron could do more than switch. It could oscillate and send out radio waves between about 100 MHz and 1 GHz. Žáček published first, but in a small journal that few people read.
events.why: It turned the magnetron from a curiosity into a source of short radio waves.

events.title: The split-anode magnetron
events.who: Kinjiro Okabe, in Hidetsugu Yagi's laboratory
events.text: Okabe, one of Yagi's first doctoral students, split the magnetron's metal cylinder into halves. This let it make much shorter waves, and he won a US patent for it in 1929. Later, in Osaka, he reached waves about 12 cm long, close to the waves in a kitchen microwave today.
events.why: Japan's early magnetron research started worldwide interest in centimetre waves.

events.title: Cooking with a radio transmitter
events.where: Century of Progress World's Fair, Chicago, USA
events.text: Westinghouse cooked food between two metal plates connected to a 10 kW shortwave radio transmitter. The waves were about 5 m long, at 60 MHz, far longer than a modern microwave oven's.
events.why: It showed that radio energy could heat food, years before anyone had a small, powerful source of shorter waves.

events.title: A cavity magnetron that nobody wanted
events.text: Hollmann patented a magnetron with several resonant cavities, an early version of the design that would later change radar. The German military turned it down because its frequency drifted, and built radar with a different tube instead.
events.why: Good ideas need the right moment: the cavity idea only took off five years later in England.

events.title: The cavity magnetron
events.where: Poynting Physics Building, University of Birmingham, England
events.text: Randall and Boot drilled holes around a solid copper block so it rang with microwaves, a bit like blowing across a bottle. When they switched it on, it made about 400 W at a wavelength of about 10 cm, around a hundred times more than earlier tubes at that wavelength. Within weeks, engineers pushed it past 1 kW.
events.why: Every microwave oven's magnetron is a descendant of this copper block.

events.title: The secret crosses the Atlantic
events.who: The Tizard Mission, with Edward ‘Taffy’ Bowen
events.text: Britain sent a team of scientists to share its war secrets with the United States. The Welsh physicist Bowen carried cavity magnetron number 12 in a box. On 19 September it was shown working to astonished American scientists, whose best tubes made far less power at those wavelengths.
events.why: An American historian later called it “the most valuable cargo ever brought to our shores”.

events.title: A laboratory for radar
events.who: MIT Radiation Laboratory and Bell Labs
events.text: Within weeks of the demonstration, the Radiation Laboratory opened at MIT to build microwave radar around the magnetron. Bell Telephone made its first 30 magnetrons that October. By the end of the war, almost every Allied radar used one.
events.why: Thousands of scientists and engineers learned to work with microwaves, and some later brought that knowledge to the kitchen.

events.title: Magnetrons by the thousand
events.text: Carving each magnetron from solid copper was slow. Spencer, Raytheon's self-taught chief engineer, found a way to stamp out thin copper pieces and join them, and output rose to about 2,600 a day. By 1945 Raytheon had built about 80% of all the magnetrons made.
events.why: Mass production made magnetrons cheap and familiar, the first step toward one in every home.

events.title: The melted candy bar
events.text: The famous story says Spencer was standing near a working radar magnetron when a candy bar in his pocket melted. No reliable first-hand record of it exists. He then tried popcorn kernels, which popped, and an egg, which exploded, reportedly in a colleague's face.
events.why: Whatever really happened, Spencer saw that microwaves could cook, and Raytheon decided to sell ovens.

events.title: A patent for cooking with microwaves
events.text: Raytheon filed Spencer's patent, ‘Method of Treating Foodstuffs’, for cooking with waves about 10 cm long. It said an egg could be hard-boiled with about 2 kilowatt-seconds of energy, compared with 36 on a normal stove. It was granted in 1950 as US patent 2,495,429.
events.why: It described cooking with microwaves from a magnetron, the idea inside every microwave oven.

events.title: A frequency for cooking
events.who: The US FCC and the International Telecommunication Union
events.where: Washington, and Atlantic City, New Jersey, USA
events.text: On 30 December 1946 the US Federal Communications Commission approved 2,450 MHz for microwave cooking. In 1947 an international radio conference in Atlantic City set aside bands for industrial, scientific and medical use, and the American delegation proposed 2.4 GHz for microwave heating. Kitchen ovens still use 2.45 GHz, with waves about 12 cm long.
events.why: Ovens got their own slice of the radio spectrum, which Wi-Fi and Bluetooth now share.

events.title: The Radarange
events.text: The first microwave oven for sale was almost 1.8 m tall and weighed about 340 kg. It used 3 kW of power, about three times a modern oven, and its magnetron was cooled with water. It cost about $5,000, and went to restaurants, ships and railway dining cars. Its name won a Raytheon staff contest.
events.why: It proved microwave cooking worked, even if no family could fit or afford one.

events.title: The first oven for homes
events.where: Mansfield, Ohio, and New York, USA
events.text: Tappan licensed Raytheon's patents in 1952 and showed an ‘Electronic Oven’ for homes in New York on 27 October 1955. It sold for about $1,300, and few families bought one.
events.why: The home microwave was possible, but it was still too big and costly.

events.title: Japan's first microwave oven
events.text: Sharp developed Japan's first microwave oven, the R-10, in 1961, and in 1962 began making them in large numbers. Toshiba also began production in 1962. Sharp sold them to businesses first, because people doubted they would ever cook without a flame at home.
events.why: Japan began to become the centre of microwave oven making.

events.title: The turntable
events.text: Sharp's R-600 put the food on a spinning plate. Microwaves bounce around the box and leave hot and cold spots, so turning the food spreads the heat more evenly. American ovens instead used a spinning metal stirrer in the roof.
events.why: The turntable became the standard design found in most microwave ovens today.

events.title: A microwave on the countertop
events.text: Raytheon bought the appliance maker Amana in 1965, and in 1967 it launched a Radarange small enough for the kitchen counter that plugged into an ordinary wall socket. It cost $495, still a lot of money. A cheap magnetron, developed with Raytheon's Japanese partner New Japan Radio, helped bring the price down.
events.why: It is widely considered the first popular home microwave oven.

events.title: Rules to keep the waves inside
events.who: US Congress and the Food and Drug Administration
events.text: The Radiation Control for Health and Safety Act of 1968 let the US government set limits for products that give off radiation. From 6 October 1971, new ovens could leak no more than 1 mW per square centimetre, measured 5 cm away, and 5 mW over their whole life. Every door needs two separate interlocks that stop the microwaves the moment it opens.
events.why: Clear, strict limits helped calm fears and let the microwave into millions of homes.

events.title: Japan makes the world's magnetrons
events.who: Toshiba, Matsushita, Hitachi and New Japan Radio
events.text: After Raytheon's basic magnetron patent ran out, several Japanese companies began making magnetrons for ovens, and Japan sold 380,000 ovens in 1969 alone. In 1971 Toshiba magnetrons went into Litton ovens in the US. Over the next decade the American magnetron makers stopped, and a few Japanese firms supplied almost the whole world.
events.why: Cheap, reliable Japanese magnetrons made the home microwave affordable everywhere.

events.title: A microwave with a computer inside
events.text: Amana added an automatic defrost setting in 1974. In 1975 its RR-6 model became the first microwave with a microprocessor and a digital touch panel instead of a turning dial.
events.why: The beeping number pad on today's microwaves began here.

events.title: Microwave popcorn
events.who: William Brastad, James Watkins and Golden Valley Microwave Foods
events.text: In 1981 a General Mills patent by Brastad described a very thin metal coating on film that turns microwaves into heat to brown food, now called a susceptor. In 1984 Golden Valley Microwave Foods launched Act II, the first mass-marketed microwave popcorn that could sit on a shelf, in a bag invented by the former Pillsbury engineer James Watkins.
events.why: Popcorn, Spencer's first test food, became the snack most linked with the microwave.

events.title: Real cooking in a microwave
events.text: Kafka, a food writer who had not used a microwave until 1984, published ‘Microwave Gourmet’. It showed serious cooks that the oven could do much more than reheat leftovers, even though many food lovers were horrified.
events.why: It helped turn the microwave from a reheating box into a cooking tool.

events.title: The inverter microwave
events.text: Most ovens make ‘half power’ by switching the magnetron fully on and off every few seconds. Panasonic's inverter used electronics to run the magnetron at a steady lower power instead. The first model gave up to 700 W.
events.why: Steady, gentle power heats food more evenly, and many ovens now work this way.

events.title: China becomes the microwave factory
events.text: Galanz, a company that began in 1978 making other goods, started making microwave ovens in 1992. By 1998 it was the biggest microwave maker in the world, with about 40% of the global market. By 2019 it was making about half of the world's microwaves.
events.why: Huge factories in China made microwave ovens cheap enough for families around the world.

events.title: India warms up to the microwave
events.text: Only about 5% of Indian households owned a microwave oven in 2013, far fewer than owned a fridge. Sales are growing as cities grow, and one market research firm valued India's microwave market at about US$572 million in 2025. Convection models that can also bake and grill are popular.
events.why: The microwave is still spreading, and much of its next growth is in Asia.

people.name: James Clerk Maxwell
people.note: Predicted that electricity and magnetism travel together as waves, including ones we cannot see.

people.name: Heinrich Hertz
people.note: First to make and detect electromagnetic waves on purpose.

people.name: Jagadish Chandra Bose
people.note: Made and detected millimetre waves in Calcutta in the 1890s, with antennas and detectors he built himself.

people.name: Albert W. Hull
people.note: Studied the magnetron at General Electric in 1921.

people.name: August Žáček
people.note: Found in 1924 that a magnetron could make radio waves, and patented his design.

people.name: Kinjiro Okabe
people.note: Invented the split-anode magnetron and reached waves about 12 cm long.

people.name: Hidetsugu Yagi
people.note: Led the Tohoku lab where Okabe did his magnetron work; best known for the Yagi-Uda antenna.

people.name: John Randall
people.note: Co-invented the cavity magnetron; later led the King's College lab where Rosalind Franklin studied DNA.

people.name: Harry Boot
people.note: Co-invented the cavity magnetron with Randall as a young researcher.

people.name: Percy Spencer
people.note: Left school early, taught himself, sped up magnetron production and patented microwave cooking.

people.name: Barbara Kafka
people.note: Her 1987 ‘Microwave Gourmet’ showed that microwaves could really cook.

series.caption: US government household surveys show the microwave going from rare to almost everywhere in about 30 years.

facts: Percy Spencer reportedly got a bonus of just $2 for his microwave cooking patent.
Kitchen microwaves use waves about 12 cm long. Melt a plate of chocolate with the turntable removed, measure the gap between melted spots (half a wave), and you can estimate the speed of light.
The metal mesh in the oven door has holes far smaller than the 12 cm microwaves, so light gets out and microwaves do not.
Microwave ovens and Wi-Fi share the same 2.4 GHz band, which is why a running microwave can slow down nearby Wi-Fi.
By 2019 one Chinese company, Galanz, was making about half of all the world's microwave ovens.
